column4: The section joins the source roots خ ل ق and ق و م in human creation and upright religion; this ayah joins Allah's creation of people on fitrah, the command to turn one's face toward religion, and dīn al-qayyim. Its “no change in Allah's creation” makes the claimed fitrah-religion alignment explicit.

The source names taqwīm as an upright, well-set human constitution; here God says He created the person, then “فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ” (proportioned and balanced you). The neighboring 82:8 completes the act by saying He assembled the person in whatever form He willed.

This ayah completes 82:7's creation and balancing: “فِي أَيِّ صُورَةٍ مَّا شَاءَ رَكَّبَكَ” says God composed the human in the form He willed. It specifies the formed human behind the section's “best taqwīm.”

The section explicitly connects its account of creation and moral direction to this next claim in the same surah: “بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ.” Here denial of dīn follows the forming in 82:7–8, matching the section's movement from upright creation to denial.

The section cites the Prophet being commanded to call his religion “دِينًا قِيَمًا” and Abraham's hanīf way; this ayah states both in its own command. It supplies a concrete prophetic model for the upright religion named by the source's ق و م dictionary form.

The section specifically points to this ending, “وَذَٰلِكَ دِينُ ٱلْقَيِّمَةِ.” The ayah describes sincere worship, prayer, and zakah as what they were commanded, so upright religion appears as lived obedience.

The source's dictionary form “al-dīn al-qayyim” is directly echoed by “ذَٰلِكَ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ.” In this ayah the phrase follows the claim that judgment belongs to God alone and that worship is for Him, joining upright religion to divine authority.

“ذَٰلِكَ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ” is the exact upright-religion phrase named in the section; its context then forbids people to wrong themselves in the sacred months. This gives the upright course a concrete ethical boundary.

The section says a person's istiqāma is staying with the straight course; here the command is to set one's face toward the upright religion before a day that cannot be turned away. It joins the source's orientation image to steadfast practice and judgment.

Like the source's explanation of the command to turn the face toward religion in 30:30, this command tells the Prophet to set his face toward the religion as a hanīf and not be among the associators. It makes the orientation a committed religious stance.

This ayah says the same religion was enjoined on Noah, Muhammad, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, and commands “أَنْ أَقِيمُوا الدِّينَ” (establish the religion). It makes the section's upright religion a continuous prophetic way rather than a merely personal disposition.

The Prophet is commanded to invite, remain upright as commanded, not follow people's desires, and “أُمِرْتُ لِأَعْدِلَ بَيْنَكُم” (be just among you). It brings together the section's straight course, obedience, and q-w-m dictionary branch of justice.

God calls this His straight path, commands people to follow it, and warns against other paths that divide them from it. This makes the section's “upright religion” an actual course of conduct with a defined opposite.

The Qur'an is said to guide to what is most upright and to give believers who do good deeds news of a great reward. This directly links the source's upright way to the faithful action and reward of 95:6.

Those who say their Lord is God and then remain upright receive the angels' reassurance. This gives the source's istikāma (adherence to the straight course) a specific form: steadfastness after professing faith.

The Prophet is told “فَٱسْتَقِمْ كَمَآ أُمِرْتَ” and told that those who repent with him must not transgress. The source names istiqāma as staying with the straight course; this is its direct commanded practice.
The Prophet is told to hold fast to what is revealed because he is on a straight path. The revealed guidance here makes concrete the upright religious direction the source traces from human creation.

The source names the ق و م dictionary form “al-qawām” as justice; this ayah commands believers to be “قَوَّامِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ,” standing firmly for justice even against themselves or kin. It shows justice as a practiced form of uprightness.

The source names “al-qawām” as justice; this ayah commands believers to be “قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ شُهَدَاءَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ” and not let hatred make them unjust. Justice is the upright boundary that holds even under pressure.
The ayah describes God as “قَائِمًا بِٱلْقِسْطِ” (upholding justice). This directly activates the source's ق و م branch connecting standing/uprightness with justice, and presents God as its ground.

The source's dictionary form “qiwām” means a support by which something stands; this ayah says God made the sacred House “قِيَامًا لِّلنَّاسِ” (a support for people), along with the sacred months and offerings. It gives that secondary support-sense a concrete communal instance.

The source names qiwām as what allows a thing to stand; this ayah calls people's property “قِيَامًا لَّكُمْ,” a means by which their lives are maintained. The link is the dictionary's support-sense, not the ayah's use of “upright religion.”

The section's dictionary form for qayyim includes a person who manages a people's affairs and sets them right; this ayah uses the related plural “قَوَّامُونَ” for men's responsibility toward women, explaining it through provision and responsibility. The family setting makes the management branch concrete.

The source defines qayyim as one who manages and sets right; this ayah calls God “قَائِمٌ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ نَفْسٍ” (watching over every soul) and its deeds. It is a related overseeing sense, not the source's upright-religion use.

The source says religion and truth stand by their support; this ayah names God “ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ” and says neither sleep nor slumber overtakes Him. It presents God as the sustaining ground behind all that stands.

The source labels the dictionary form خُلُق as innate disposition or character; this ayah calls the Prophet's character “خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ.” It makes the section's move from created nature to an established moral disposition concrete.

The source labels خُلُق as an innate habit or disposition; this ayah uses “خُلُقُ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ” for the way of earlier peoples (often rendered their custom). That secondary customary sense links a settled way of life with the section's neighboring dictionary sense of dīn as habit or condition.

The source labels خُلُق as disposition; this ayah says each acts according to “شَاكِلَتِهِ” (his manner or disposition), while God knows best who is guided. It supplies a nonlexical parallel for how a person's settled nature appears in conduct.

God makes humanity testify that He is their Lord before they enter ordinary life, so they cannot plead ignorance. This gives the source's fitrah claim a specific Quranic scene of an original recognition of God.

The source names 30:30's “no change in Allah's creation” as part of the fitrah link; Satan here threatens to command people to “فَلَيُغَيِّرُنَّ خَلْقَ ٱللَّهِ” (change Allah's creation). The ayah voices the opposing pressure against the created orientation; the context is Satan's promise, not an endorsement of it.

Abraham turns his face toward the One who created the heavens and earth as a hanīf, rejecting association. This is a direct scene of orientation to the Creator that parallels the source's fitrah and face-to-religion link.

The Prophet is told to follow Abraham's religion as a hanīf, and Abraham is said not to have been among the associators. It gives the section's “upright religion” a concrete inherited model of exclusive devotion.

This ayah calls the one who submits his face to God while doing good and follows Abraham's hanīf way the best in religion. The joined face, religion, and good action echo the section's orientation toward upright religion and its faithful deeds.

The ayah says righteousness is not merely turning faces east or west, then describes faith, giving, prayer, covenant-keeping, and patience. It clarifies how the source's face-oriented religion becomes a whole pattern of righteous conduct.
God swears by the soul and the One who proportioned it. The source's “best taqwīm” is a well-formed human constitution; this ayah makes the soul's formation the starting point of moral direction.

The formed soul is made to know its wickedness and its piety. This gives a moral counterpart to the source's claim that created human nature is oriented toward the straight religion, while keeping both possible directions in view.
The soul succeeds through its purification. This makes the source's exception for those who believe and do righteous deeds (95:6) a specific act of moral cultivation.
The soul fails when it is buried or corrupted. This is a direct moral reversal of 91:9's purification and illuminates the section's descent from upright constitution to a lower condition.

God creates and proportionately forms all things; for the human image, 87:2 continues in 87:3 with measuring and guiding. This is a close parallel to the source's paired ideas of human creation and taqwīm.
This completes 87:2's created and proportioned order: God measures and guides. It connects formed nature to direction, the same link the source draws between fitrah and dīn al-qayyim.

After recounting the stages of human development, this ayah says the human is brought forth as another creation. That formed human is a specific creation parallel to the source's “best taqwīm,” though it does not itself state the moral direction.

After creation from clay and the human lineage, God fashions the person, breathes of His spirit, and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, yet few are grateful. It connects formed human capacities with the moral response central to the source's shift from creation to faith and deeds.

God created people, yet some disbelieve and some believe. This directly places the section's created human and subsequent faith or denial on the same axis; creation does not erase the moral divergence.
God creates the heavens and earth, fashions people beautifully, and says the return is to Him. It joins the source's beautifully ordered human creation to accountability.

This ayah says God fashioned people and made their forms good, after making the earth a dwelling and the sky a canopy. It is a direct parallel to the source's formed human, though it does not itself develop the later moral reversal.

God says He honored the children of Adam, carried them, provided for them, and preferred them over many creatures. This places the source's descent to “the lowest” against an explicit Quranic statement of human dignity.

People who fail to use their hearts, eyes, and ears are compared to cattle and said to be even more astray. This is a specific Quranic picture of human capacities falling below their proper use, illuminating the source's descent from the best constitution.
Those who refuse guidance are likened to cattle, or further astray, and called heedless. This sharpens the source's contrast between the formed human and the low state that follows rejection.

The neighboring 98:7 calls believers with righteous deeds “خَيْرُ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ”; this ayah calls the disbelievers among the People of the Book and polytheists “شَرُّ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ.” The paired ranking makes the section's fall and its faithful exception concrete; this row states the negative side.

This ayah calls those who believe and do righteous deeds “خَيْرُ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ,” while the preceding 98:6 names disbelievers “شَرُّ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ.” It directly parallels 95:6's exception of faithful doers from the low condition.
This completes 98:7's description of the faithful as the best of creatures by naming their reward: gardens of lasting residence and God's approval. It parallels the source's believers' uncut reward.

The one who transgresses is set at the head of a passage ending in Hell for those who prefer worldly life (79:38–39). This gives a specific moral route toward ruin that contrasts with the faithful exception in the source.

This ayah specifies the preference for worldly life as the transgressor's orientation; 79:37 names the transgression and 79:39 its Hell consequence. It offers a concrete contrary direction to the source's upright faith and righteous work.

Hell is the destination completing 79:37–38's transgression and preference for worldly life. It gives the downward outcome in that passage separately from the source's promised uncut reward for the faithful.

The contrasting person fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire. This is a concrete inner discipline that leads away from the downward route and complements the section's faith and righteous acts.
Paradise is the destination completing 79:40's restraint of desire, in contrast with 79:37–39. It gives a specific lasting outcome for a person whose conduct stays oriented to God.

This ayah says people prefer the nearer worldly life; the next says the Hereafter is better and more enduring. That preference supplies a concrete contrary orientation to the enduring reward promised to the faithful in the source.
The Hereafter is “خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ” (better and more lasting), completing 87:16's preference for worldly life. This directly clarifies the lasting side of the source's “uninterrupted” reward.

Whoever turns away from God's remembrance is promised a constricted life and will be raised blind. This specifies a consequence of turning away that illuminates the source's movement from created orientation to a low condition.

The ayah describes someone who makes desire his god, then has hearing and heart sealed and sight covered. It is a particular way the created human capacities can be turned from their intended guidance, matching the source's moral descent.

The source explicitly names this verse for the root ر د د: some People of the Book wish to turn believers into disbelievers “مِّنۢ بَعْدِ إِيمَٰنِكُمْ.” Its own context makes the source's “after” link and reversal of faith explicit.

The source explicitly cites this answer about fighting in the sacred month: opponents seek to turn believers from their religion, and whoever turns from it is named. It gives the exact religious-apostasy setting that the source's r-d-d dictionary note evokes.
The source cites the warning that some seek to turn believers into disbelievers “بَعْدَ إِيمَٰنِكُمْ.” This directly joins the root ر د د named in the source to its “after faith” sequence.

This ayah asks how God would guide people who disbelieved after believing and bearing witness to the Messenger's truth. Its “after their faith” sequence is a close parallel to the source's word بعد and its return-from-faith examples.

After the preceding account of people who disbelieved after faith, this ayah makes an exception for those who repent and mend their ways. It parallels the source's distinction between a fall and a faithful, righteous exception.

This ayah explicitly describes disbelief “after his faith,” while excepting the person compelled whose heart remains secure in faith. It directly echoes the source's post-faith reversal and preserves an important exception in the ayah's own context.

The ayah asks who among believers would turn back from their religion, then describes God bringing a people He loves who love Him. It gives both the apostasy sense of the source's r-d-d note and a response to that reversal.

This ayah describes people who turn back after guidance has become clear, with Satan making it seem easy to them. It directly parallels the source's movement from upright guidance toward return and denial.

After the Prophet's death, the ayah asks whether people would turn back on their heels. It is a specific reversal after faith, though the verse frames it as a question rather than asserting that the believers do so.
Believers are warned that obeying disbelievers would make them turn back on their heels and become losers. This gives the source's return-to-disbelief image a concrete social pressure and outcome.

The source's root ر د د dictionary note describes returning oneself to disbelief; this ayah uses the same root to command disputed matters to be referred back to God and the Messenger. The contrasting return shows the root can also name a corrective return to religious authority.

This ayah describes people believing, disbelieving, believing again, and disbelieving again, then increasing in disbelief. It makes the section's return-from-faith image a repeated pattern, using the different but concrete wording of alternating faith and denial.

This ayah repeats the source's exception almost word for word: those who believe and do righteous deeds have “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.” It specifies that the reward is not cut off, exactly clarifying the phrase in 95:6.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are promised “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ,” the same uncut reward named in the source's 95:6. It confirms the reward as a repeated Quranic promise to this group.

The people addressed say they are only reformers while being told not to cause corruption; 2:12 answers that they are the corrupters, though unaware. This concretely activates the source's definition of ṣalāḥ as the opposite of fasād in deeds.
This ayah exposes the contradiction in 2:11: the people who claim to reform are in fact corrupters. It supplies the negative side of the source's ṣ-l-ḥ / fasād distinction.

The person who turns away strives to spread corruption and destroy crops and offspring, and God does not love corruption. This puts the source's opposition between righteous deeds and corruption into a concrete pattern of action.

The ayah forbids corruption on earth after it has been set right. It uses the same repair-versus-corruption relationship as the source's ṣ-l-ḥ dictionary definition and connects good deeds to maintaining what is sound.
Moses says that God does not set right the work of corrupters. The ayah applies the source's ṣalāḥ/fasād opposition directly to people's actions, although its scene is Moses confronting sorcery.

The ayah says the Lord would not destroy towns unjustly while their people were setting things right. It connects righteous conduct with judgment, the two ideas joined in the source's faith, good works, and dīn.

The source reads dīn in 95:7 as a settled religious way while the whole surah's closing judgment question also leaves the judgment sense in view. This ayah names God “مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ,” making that reckoning sense explicit.

The ayah swears that “إِنَّ ٱلدِّينَ لَوَاقِعٌ” (the Judgment will surely occur). This directly activates the judgment sense of dīn that can be heard in the source's question after creation and moral action.
After 82:9's denial of dīn, this ayah says the wicked enter the Fire on the Day of Judgment. It supplies the consequence in the same surah; 82:16 adds that they will not be absent from it.
This completes 82:15 by saying the wicked will not be absent from the Fire on the Day of Judgment. It makes the judgment denied in 82:9 an unavoidable outcome.
The ayah asks what will make people know the Day of Judgment, after 82:15–16 have named its Fire and permanence. It explicitly repeats the dīn of 82:9 as a coming reckoning.
This repeats the question about the Day of Judgment and heightens the warning begun in 82:17. The sequence makes the denied dīn from 82:9 concrete as an approaching event.

The ayah explains that on the Day of Judgment no soul can help another and all command belongs to God. It completes the same surah's warning against denying dīn in 82:9 with the judgment's actual condition.
This ayah describes people who deny “بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ.” It is a direct Qur'anic formulation of the judgment-sense of dīn that the section's final question can carry.

The denier of dīn is identified by what follows: repelling the orphan and failing to urge the feeding of the poor (107:2–3). This links dīn as judgment or religion to the ethical conduct the section associates with righteous works.

The ayah rejects the idea that humans were created without purpose or would not be returned to God. It joins creation directly to return and accountability, clarifying why the source moves from human formation to dīn.

The ayah asks whether a human thinks he will be left without responsibility, then 75:37–40 recount origin and formation and God's power to resurrect. It makes created human form answerable to the coming judgment.
This names the human's origin as a drop, beginning 75:37–40's argument that the One who formed him can resurrect him. It gives a concrete creation-to-accountability parallel to the source's sequence.
This says the drop became a clinging form and was then proportioned; 75:37 and 75:39–40 complete the creation-to-resurrection argument. The formed body links to the source's human constitution.

This says God made the human pair male and female, completing the account of formation that grounds 75:40's resurrection question. It supplies another specific part of human creation behind accountability.
The surah concludes its account of human origin and formation by asking whether the Creator cannot bring the dead to life. It joins creation to the judgment and return implied by the source's dīn.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God sincerely in dīn. This makes the source's dictionary sense of dīn as obedience concrete as exclusive worship.
The Prophet says he worships God, making his religion sincere for Him alone. It is a direct lived instance of the source's dīn-as-obedience sense.
The ayah says worship belongs to God alone and that dīn belongs to Him enduringly. This directly supports the source's dictionary sense of dīn as obedience and an established religious way.

When believers are called to God and the Messenger for judgment, their answer is that they hear and obey. This gives a concrete instance of the source's dīn-as-obedience sense; the call to judgment is stated in 24:48–50.
God identifies the straight path as His way and says its signs have been detailed. This is a direct repeated formulation of the source's straight-course sense of istiqāma.
Revelation is described as a light by which God guides to a straight path. It makes the source's upright religious direction concrete as revealed guidance.
The worshippers ask God to guide them to the straight path. This is a direct devotional formulation of the upright course named in the source.
God says He commanded the children of Adam not to worship Satan but to worship Him, “this is a straight path.” The verse joins obedience to the source's straight-course image.
Jesus says God is his Lord and theirs, commands worship of Him, and calls this the straight path. This joins the source's dīn-as-obedience sense to a direct formulation of the upright way.
The ayah says whoever holds fast to God has been guided to a straight path. It gives a specific means of remaining on the upright course described in the source.
God says the straight course belongs to Him while some paths deviate. This gives the source's straight religious way a specific contrast between guidance and deviation.
When challenged to become Jews or Christians to be guided, the answer is to follow Abraham's hanīf way. It is a direct repeated formulation of the upright Abrahamic religion named in the source.
The ayah commands people to follow Abraham's way as a hanīf. It directly supplies another Quranic formulation of the source's hanīf, upright religion.

Abraham is described as neither Jew nor Christian but a hanīf who submitted to God, not an associator. This specifies the religious orientation named in the source and distinguishes it from later labels.

The ayah asks who would turn away from Abraham's way except someone who makes a foolish choice, then says God chose him. It supplies a concrete turning away from the hanīf course described in the source.

In a parable, one figure commands justice and is on a straight path. This brings together the source's q-w-m dictionary branches of justice and uprightness, with the scene contrasting that person with a helpless dependent.

Shuayb commands his people to give full measure and not spread corruption on earth after it has been set right. This joins the source's ṣ-l-ḥ versus fasād distinction to just action in a concrete setting.
In its discussion of orphans, the ayah says God knows the corrupter from the reformer. It directly activates the source's dictionary explanation of ṣalāḥ as the opposite of fasād in deeds.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are said to have their misdeeds removed and their condition set right. This links the source's faith and ṣāliḥ deeds to God's setting the believers right.
Moses says God gave each thing its created form and then guided it. This is a specific parallel to the source's link between creation and the direction appropriate to that creation.

If “asfala sāfilīn” in the source also allows the bodily reading of decline in old age, this ayah gives a specific parallel: God creates people, then some reach the most decrepit age and lose knowledge. That reading is not developed in the section, so the connection is uncertain.

If the source's descent to “asfala sāfilīn” includes bodily decline, this ayah's human arc from weakness to strength and back to weakness is a concrete parallel. The section itself emphasizes religious direction, so this reading remains uncertain.

If the source's “lowest of the low” is read as an ultimate condemned station, this ayah places hypocrites in the lowest depths of the Fire. That interpretation is not developed in the source section, so the connection is uncertain.
The speakers say they used to deny the Day of Judgment. This is a direct denial formulation for the judgment-sense of dīn that can be heard in the source's closing question.
The resurrected say this is the Day of Judgment. It directly activates dīn as reckoning in a scene of resurrection and accountability.
This identifies the Day of Separation and says it is the day people denied, completing 37:20's Day of Judgment. It directly links the source's denial question to its judgment sense.
After naming deniers of the Day of Judgment in 83:11, this ayah specifies that the denier is every transgressing sinner. It links rejection of dīn to a concrete moral condition.
This says that when the revelations are recited to the deniers, they call them tales of earlier people. It adds the deniers' response to the judgment-denial named in 83:11.

The ayah says what people have earned has covered their hearts. In the surrounding passage about denying the Day of Judgment, it makes conduct a cause of spiritual obscuration, complementing the source's faith-and-deeds distinction.
This says the deniers will be screened from their Lord on that day. It gives a consequence completing the judgment passage that begins by naming denial of the Day of Judgment in 83:11.

The denier of dīn is identified in the next ayah as one who repels the orphan. This gives the source's link between religion and righteous action a concrete social example; 107:1 names the denial itself.
The denier of dīn is also one who does not urge feeding the poor. This gives the source's dīn-as-lived-obedience and righteous-deeds themes a concrete social example; 107:1 names the denial itself.

The ayah asks whether a human does not see that God created him from a drop, yet he becomes a clear opponent. It is a specific creation-to-denial parallel to the source's movement from human formation to denial of dīn.

The human who disputes resurrection forgets his own creation and asks who will revive decayed bones. This supplies the challenge that 36:79 answers, paralleling the source's movement from creation to a question of judgment.
The answer is that the One who produced the bones the first time will revive them. It completes 36:78 and directly joins original creation to return, clarifying the accountability behind dīn.
The ayah says God gives life and death and will gather people on the Day of Resurrection, of which there is no doubt. It directly joins creation and human life to the judgment-sense of dīn.
The ayah says whoever does good does so for himself and whoever does evil does so against himself, then all return to God. It connects the source's righteous deeds to an individual reckoning.

God makes believers firm with the firm word in this life and the Hereafter. This is a specific support-and-steadfastness parallel to the source's q-w-m senses of a sustaining foundation and adherence to the straight course.
